office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The 'Fulton Rochester School Board' races on the state list are for Rochester Community School Corporation in Rochester, Fulton County [6, 24]. The district says it serves about 1,400 students in The Learning Center, Columbia Elementary (PreK-1), Riddle Elementary (grades 2-4), Rochester Middle School (grades 5-7) and Rochester High School (grades 8-12) [25].

The superintendent is Jana Vance [26]. In August 2025 she said she was in her 11th year as superintendent. Before that she was a teacher, guidance counselor, assistant principal and Rochester Middle School principal in the district [27].

The board has seven members. The district lists Casi Cowles (president), Katie Miller (vice president), Jennie Smith (secretary), Mark Martens, Kyle Rensberger, Ethan Trottier and Stephen Williams [24]. Seats are tied to areas of the district. In 2022 the Rochester Sentinel reported that Richland Township 'has a designated seat on the board' [28]. That year's ballot listed 'Rochester School Board, Dist. 1' with one candidate (Mark E. Martens) and 'Dist. 2' with 'Choose up to three' (Jennifer M. Smith, Ethan Trottier and Stephen Williams) [29]. All four were elected [30]. Cowles, Miller and Rensberger were reelected to at-large seats in 2024 [31].
District 1 (Richland) race: one seat. Mark Martens, elected to this seat in 2022, is not on the 2026 ballot, so the seat is open [29, 6]. Kalyn Ranstead is the only candidate [6].

District 2 (Rochester) race: three seats, not one. The state list says 'vote for 1' [6]. However, the three District 2 seats filled in 2022 ('Choose up to three') belong to Smith, Trottier and Williams, whose four-year terms run through 2026 [29, 30, 24]. Smith and Trottier are running again, and Williams is not on the ballot [6]. Four candidates are running [6].

Ballot-list discrepancy: the Rochester Sentinel's Oct. 3, 2026 list of Fulton County candidates labels the school board race 'At-large' and names four candidates, Michael A. Doran, Tim Durkes, Kalyn Ranstead and Jennifer Smith, without Ethan Trottier [32]. The state list places Ranstead in District 1 (Richland) and includes Trottier in District 2 [6]. The same Sentinel list names an 'Ethan Trottier, Republican' as a candidate for the Newcastle Township Advisory Board [32]. Voters should check their own ballot.

2027 budget (September-October 2026): the district advertised a 2027 budget of $21,120,000, including $12,950,000 in the Education Fund, $4,670,000 in Operations and $3,500,000 in Debt Service. The public hearing was set for Sept. 21 and adoption for Oct. 19, 2026 [33]. The notice estimates a $234,700 property-tax-cap credit [33].

Costs and state funding (August 2025): Vance said more than half of students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch (58.3 percent at Rochester) and that the district's English-learner population is growing [27]. She said state 'unfunded mandates' and rising costs for electricity, insurance and supplies were adding pressure while the district was 'not getting any help from the state.' [27]

Facilities: a $2,756,000 renovation of the Rochester Middle School natatorium was paid for with general obligation bond proceeds and was expected to be finished by the 2025-26 school year [34]. In August 2025 Vance also cited $1.2 million in roof replacements at Riddle Elementary and a planned renovation of the high school tennis courts [27].

Programs: the district reported a 100 percent graduation rate in 2024 and credited its preschool, internships and vocational programs, including CDL and heavy-equipment classes [27]. Vance said a community day care, Little Zebbie's, was being funded by a $2.5 million READI 2.0 grant, with groundbreaking planned for 2026 [27]. Starting in August 2026, students must keep phones silenced and stored in lockers during the school day to comply with state law [26].
Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire for the Rochester races.

candidates.summary: Nonpartisan candidate, unopposed, for the open Richland Township seat now held by Mark Martens, who is not running [6, 29].
path_to_ballot: The state lists her as Nonpartisan [6]. The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 12, 2026 as her filing date [35]. She has no opponent [6].
gaps: This guide found no campaign website, social media page, news coverage or questionnaire for this candidate.
Occupation, community roles and ties to Rochester schools could not be found.
The Rochester Sentinel lists her as an 'at-large' candidate, while the state lists her for the District 1 (Richland) seat. This guide could not resolve the difference.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, first elected in 2022 and seeking another term in District 2, where three seats are up [30, 24, 6].
background: Is a Rochester High School graduate who served as a student non-voting member of the Rochester Park Board [36].
In 2023 the Rochester Park Board named an Ethan Trottier as one of the managers of the city pool [37].
In January 2024, Rochester's mayor named school board member Ethan Trottier to the Rochester Redevelopment Commission, replacing board member Katie Miller [38].
path_to_ballot: Was elected to the board in November 2022 and sworn in in January 2023 [30, 39].
The state lists him as Nonpartisan [6]. The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 18, 2026 as his filing date [35].
gaps: This guide found no campaign website, campaign statements or questionnaire answers for 2026, and no news account of his votes or statements on school board business.
His current occupation could not be confirmed.

The Rochester Sentinel's Oct. 3, 2026 candidate list leaves him out of the school board race and lists an 'Ethan Trottier, Republican' for the Newcastle Township Advisory Board. This guide could not confirm whether this is the same person or whether the list contains an error.
Board minutes on BoardDocs could not be reached, so his voting record was not reviewed.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board secretary, seeking another term in District 2, where three seats are up. The board lists her as Jennie Smith [24, 28, 6].
background: The district lists 'Jennie Smith' as board secretary [24]. She was board vice president in 2020 and secretary in 2022 [40, 41].
path_to_ballot: In 2022 the Sentinel described Jennifer Smith as the only incumbent among the Rochester school board candidates, and she was reelected [28, 30].
The state lists her as Nonpartisan [6]. The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 10, 2026 as her filing date [35].

items: In May 2020, during pandemic school closures, she opposed a request to change how fourth-quarter grades would count for high school students. She said she had 'some strong concerns that this is wiping out the past nine weeks' and that 'these students use virtual learning all the time.' All six members present voted no [42].

In March 2020 the board debated whether to pay hourly staff 80 or 100 percent of their wages during the closure. She favored 80 percent so there would be an incentive for reassigned staff to come to work, and the board settled on 80 percent [43].

gaps: This guide found no campaign website, campaign statements or questionnaire answers for 2026.

The ballot name (Jennifer Roberts Smith), the 2022 ballot name (Jennifer M. Smith) and the district's listing (Jennie Smith) differ. This guide treats them as the same incumbent because the Sentinel called Jennifer Smith the only incumbent in 2022, but no source states this directly.
When she first joined the board and her occupation could not be found.
Board minutes on BoardDocs could not be reached, so her recent votes were not reviewed. The positions above are from 2020.
No campaign finance reports were found.
